# Ecological succession

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Ecological succession** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Organisms and Environment fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Ecological succession

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

**Ecological succession** is the predictable, directional change in the species composition of a community over time, ending in a stable **climax community** matched to the climate. It starts from bare rock (primary) or from a disturbed site with soil intact (secondary). The sequence of temporary communities is the **sere**; the first colonisers are **pioneers**.

**Concept flow — from bare ground to climax (study in this order)**

| Step | Stage | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Nudation | Disturbance creates a bare area (lava, flood, fire, landslide) |
| 2 | Pioneer colonisation | Lichens (rock) or hardy weeds (soil) arrive; soil begins to form |
| 3 | Sere progression | Moss → grass → shrub → young forest: each stage modifies the habitat for the next |
| 4 | Climax community | Stable, self-perpetuating community set by the climate (e.g. forest) |
| 5 | Trends throughout | Biomass, species diversity and niche specialisation all increase; net productivity rises then stabilises |

**Primary vs secondary succession; hydrarch vs xerarch**

| Feature | Primary succession | Secondary succession |
|---|---|---|
| Starting point | Bare rock, lava, sand — no soil | Disturbed site with soil intact (burnt forest, abandoned field) |
| Pioneers | Lichens, mosses | Grasses, weeds from surviving seeds |
| Speed | Very slow (thousands of years — soil must form) | Fast (decades — soil already there) |
| Example | Lava flow colonised on Hawaii | Farmland abandoned in Nepal's middle hills |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example.** A lava flow cools to bare basalt. Lichens secrete acids, etching the rock and trapping dust — the first soil. Mosses follow, then grasses, then shrubs, then trees; each stage adds organic matter and holds more water, making the site habitable for the next, larger species. Centuries later: forest. **Key insight:** succession is driven by the community modifying its own environment — the pioneers are engineers of their own replacement.

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Define succession, sere, pioneer and climax. (2) Contrast primary and secondary succession in four points. (3) Compare hydrarch and xerarch seres and note they converge on the same climax. (4) Name the pioneer of xerosere (lichens) and of hydrosere (phytoplankton). (5) State the trends: biomass, diversity, productivity.

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Succession is directional community change driven by habitat modification, from pioneer to climax; primary starts without soil and is slow, secondary with soil and is fast; water-started and rock-started seres both end in mesic forest. **Self-check:** can you list five sere stages in order for a bare rock?

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Definition: gradual, predictable change of species composition culminating in a climax community — 'directional and predictable' are the keywords.
Trick 2: Stages: pioneer → seral stages → climax; hydrarch (water → forest) vs xerarch (bare rock → forest) — both END in mesic climax, the convergence line.
Trick 3: Pioneers: lichens on rock (xerarch), phytoplankton in water (hydrarch) — the two starting species.
Trick 4: Succession increases: species diversity, biomass, NPP-to-biomass ratio changes, soil depth — the four trends.
